order: The roster puts canary-islands, then txakoli, then ribeiro-ribeira-sacra on the spain sheet, and check-fragment enforces that order, so the file holds them that way even though the task named Txakoli first.
check: check-fragment reports one problem per article and nothing else: regions[i].deeper is required for an article off the map. This edition writes no deeper list (the task's rule, as in c1 to c4), so the integrator relaxes that .more rule. With only that rule relaxed the file passes whole, with no superlative note. The articles are not deepened, so each is held to the one prose total (800 to 1,800 words, every place note counted), and each has 10 cards and 8 questions with 5 multiple choice. No key is the longest option, and the file has no dash, no glyph at or above U+2190, no numbered level and no use of the retired word.
applyRoster: A dry run of apply-roster over a copy of fragments/ plus this file finds no clash. It moves valdeorras and ribeira sacra from spain.1.json (bierzo) to ribeiro-ribeira-sacra and sets the Spain regionsOrder to the eleven map slugs, then canary-islands, txakoli and ribeiro-ribeira-sacra. Bierzo's place 'Valdeorras and Ribeira Sacra' becomes the roster's one line pointer (takes).
aliases: Every roster alias is claimed. Added for the Canary Islands: canary wine, la geria, fuencaliente, hoyo de mazo, fuerteventura, tacoronte, orotava, icod de los vinos, vilaflor. Added for Txakoli: chacoli de getaria, txakoli de getaria, chacoli de bizkaia, txakoli de bizkaia, chacoli de alava, txakoli de alava, getaria, zarautz, bakio, bizkaia, gipuzkoa, guipuzcoa, vizcaya, valle de ayala, ayala valley, aiara, amurrio, okondo, euskadi. Added for Ribeiro: ribadavia, ourense, o barco de valdeorras, o barco, a rua, chantada, quiroga bibei, ribeiras do mino, ribeiras do sil, verin, val de monterrei, ladeira de monterrei, tostado do ribeiro. Deliberately not claimed, because older fragments own them: alava and rioja alavesa (rioja), galicia (rias-baixas), irouleguy (south-west-france). The bare word canary is not claimed, since the house list prints Canary Hill, an Oregon vineyard. No Brennan's wine names any of these places (the house Godello is Bierzo's).
cats: No cats are written. The integrator may add Spain: [canary-islands, txakoli, ribeiro-ribeira-sacra] and galicia: [ribeiro-ribeira-sacra] (the Régionale Galicia primer names Ribeiro, Ribeira Sacra, Valdeorras and Monterrei); build-regions merges cats across fragments.
cms: galicia (the Court's page 37) has Certified cells for Valdeorras and Ribeira Sacra: climate maritime on the coast becoming more continental inland, steep slopes and terraced vineyards in Ribeira Sacra, granite soil, occasional barrique, Godello and Mencía, Valdeorras (Godello, Mencía) and Ribeira Sacra (Albariño and Godello, Mencía) as DOs, dry crisp whites and light reds with fresh Godello in Valdeorras. Every one is covered untagged in ribeiro-ribeira-sacra. spain-other-dos (País Vasco) has Certified cells for the Atlantic coast of northern Spain, a moderate maritime climate (Green Spain), the Atlantic Ocean, temperature-controlled stainless steel tanks, Hondarrabi Zuri and Hondarrabi Beltza, the three Txakoli DOs, a style that is mostly dry white with rare reds and rosés, lightly effervescent, high in acid and meant to be drunk young, and oily seafood as the match. Every one is covered untagged in txakoli. No CMS subject has a row for the Canary Islands. The Codex's own banks set the tags: Régionale has the Lanzarote pits, Txakoli, Valdeorras's Godello and Ribeira Sacra's terraces (all untagged); Village has Getariako first, Hondarrabi Beltza, Monterrei in the Támega valley and Treixadura in Ribeiro (untagged); Premier Cru has Listán Negro and the braided cordons (tagged advanced); Grand Cru has hoyos and zocos at La Geria, Ribeiro's medieval trade and the inland white grapes (hoyo, zoco and La Geria tagged master, the trade in an advanced place note named as a Grand Cru line in exam).

articles.name: Canary Islands
uncertain: Eleven DOs, five of them on Tenerife, with the DOP Islas Canarias (Canary Wine) recognised in 2011 (Boletín Oficial de Canarias, 11 May 2011, by a search summary); the Consejo's institutional paper and the Ministry's registration certificate are cited. No merger of Tenerife's five DOs from 2020 to 2026 turned up in one search.
Tacoronte-Acentejo as the first Canary DO, in 1992, rests on one secondary result and standard knowledge; its order was not read.
Fuerteventura's lack of a DO of its own, and the DOP Islas Canarias letting a house blend across islands, come from the Consejo's role as reported, not from the specification text.

Malvasía Volcánica as a natural crossing of Malvasía Aromática and Marmajuelo is written as the usual account: the sources agree once Bermejuela is read as Marmajuelo's other name, but no DNA study was read.

The cordón trenzado as found nowhere else rests on the La Orotava council paper and the DO's own page. How it began is disputed, so the article gives no origin, and its area figures, which conflict, are left out.

La Palma's rules (the May 2015 pliego): three subzones, Malvasía dulce from overripe grapes with more than 45 grams of sugar per litre, and vino de tea from the north of the island kept for at most six months in Canary pine. One secondary source places vino de tea at Hoyo de Mazo, and the article follows the pliego. A later amendment was not checked.
The San Antonio eruption of 1677 at Fuencaliente comes from a search result. The Cumbre Vieja eruption of September to December 2021 is left out because no source gave its effect on vineyards.
El Grifo as an eighteenth-century house with a wine museum is standard knowledge and was not searched; its founding year is left out.
Carbonic maceration for young Listán Negro on Tenerife is standard knowledge and was not searched.

Identities left out because they could not be confirmed: Gual, Vijariego, Tintilla, Baboso Negro as Alfrocheiro, and how Listán Negro relates to Listán Prieto. Negramoll as Tinta Negra and Listán Blanco as Palomino are kept (the Codex's grape data and Wine Grapes).
Figures left out: rainfall, hectares and vineyard heights beyond 'above 1,000 metres around Vilaflor'. Teide's 3,715 metres is given without calling it the highest.

articles.name: Txakoli and the Basque Country
uncertain: Getariako Txakolina: the order of 21 September 1989 (BOPV, 25 October 1989) for Getaria, Zarautz and Aia, and the order of 27 April 2007 that extended it to all of Gipuzkoa (the 2011 pliego, the BOE text of 2 January 2010 and the Consejo's press dossier). Bizkaiko Txakolina 1994. Arabako Txakolina 2001 in most sources, 2002 in one.

The permitted grapes differ by DO and by the date of the text, so the article names them with no shares. Getaria's 2011 pliego lists Hondarrabi Zuri Zerratia (Petit Courbu), Izkiriota (Gros Manseng), Riesling and Chardonnay, capped together at 20 per cent of a winery's vineyard. Bizkaia's 2024 consolidated pliego caps Folle Blanche (Mune Mahatsa) at 20 per cent. Petit Manseng and Sauvignon Blanc in Bizkaia, and Petit Manseng in Álava, each rest on one secondary source.

Amendments from 2020 to 2026 were seen only as search summaries: Bizkaia's of 2024 and 2025 (a description of its wines), Álava's of 2025 (the spelling of Hondarrabi, with sparkling already in its pliego) and a 2024 change to the traditional term Chacolí, Txakolina, Txakoli. None is written as a rule. Sparkling and barrel-aged txakoli are described only as the work of a growing number of houses.
That Hondarrabi Beltza grows mostly around Bakio rests on one secondary source and is left out; Bakio is written only as a historic centre of Bizkaia's txakoli.

The Ayala valley's climate (colder winters with snow, spring frost, a little less rain) rests on regional tourism and wine-guide sources; its rainfall figure, the heights and all hectares are left out.
Txomin Etxaniz, a classic Getaria house, is left out because its trading name is a person's name and it is not known whether that person is living.
Rioja Alavesa (untagged) and Irouléguy (tagged advanced) are pointer places; their aliases stay with rioja and south-west-france.

articles.name: Ribeiro, Ribeira Sacra and Valdeorras
uncertain: Valdeorras's DO date conflicts: 1945 in most secondary sources, a ministerial order of 30 July 1957 in the Xunta's 2025 technical sheet, and 1997 in the Interprofesional's list. The article leaves it undated, as recognised in the middle of the century and Galicia's second DO after Ribeiro, which holds whichever date is right.

Ribeiro 1932 under the Estatuto del Vino rests on the Interprofesional and the reference summaries; Monterrei 1994 and Ribeira Sacra 1996 rest on the Interprofesional and the Xunta (the Diario Oficial de Galicia of 11 September 1996).

Ribeiro's 2025 pliego (April 2025; EU approval DOUE C/2025/6457 of 4 December 2025, by the 2025 technical sheet) adds a quality sparkling wine made by the traditional method from the preferred native grapes, Brut or Brut Nature, and divides still wines into those of the preferred grapes ('Ribeiro castes', by the search summary) and those of secondary grapes. The label term is not given in the article because only a summary showed it.

Ribeira Sacra's 2025 amendment (resolution of 7 February 2025; EU OJ C/2025/2949 of 28 May 2025): one press report says it limits new planting and changes the yields for reds. The article says only that it limits new planting, and gives no yield figure.
ReViVal is dated to 1974 by most sources and to 1976 to 1977 by one; the agronomist behind it is not named. Godeval is written as founded in the 1980s (two sources mark its fortieth year in 2026).

Merenzao as Trousseau and Bastardo rests on Wine Grapes and the Monterrei documents. Treixadura as Trajadura and Loureira as Loureiro come from the Codex's Village bank. That Galician Torrontés is a different vine from Argentina's is standard knowledge and was not searched.

The subzone notes are standard knowledge: Amandi's south-facing slate on the Sil's north bank in Lugo, Chantada on granite, Quiroga-Bibei to the east and warmer. Ribeiras do Miño and Ribeiras do Sil are kept general. The rack railways and the boat access are written loosely ('small rack railways', 'once reached by boat').

Tostado: the 2004 order names the white grapes, so a red Tostado is not claimed. Ribeiro's trade with England in the late Middle Ages comes from the reference works and the Codex's Grand Cru bank, and sits in Ribadavia's advanced place note.

Producers: Guitián is the brand of Bodegas A Tapada, a family name and not a person's full name. Rafael Palacios (p-rafael-palacios), a living person's name, is left out. Ponte da Boga's founding year is left out because it is unconfirmed.
